# Frozen development lessons, version 1

These rules were curated with Codex assistance from official training runs.
They contain no task answers and are not updated during held-out evaluation.

## L1: Stop searching after confirming an unavailable external dataset

When execution fails on a network request, inspect the loader and check the
provided data directory once. If the required dataset is neither bundled nor
cached, record the failing request and submit unanswered values with blocker
evidence. Do not repeatedly search the entire filesystem or try alternative
internet endpoints in an offline environment.

## L2: Execute a notebook once and inspect its structured outputs

For notebook reproduction, save an executed notebook in the results directory,
then render that executed notebook to the requested presentation format. Locate
relevant output cells using the requested metric labels. Print only the needed
output segments. Avoid dumping full notebook source or raw HTML into context,
and avoid executing the whole experiment again merely to read its output.

instruction file is actually provided and read REPRODUCING.md separately. A
missing optional README should not prevent required instructions from being read.

available files and recovered.

## Scope

These are development-derived workflow heuristics, not verified universal rules.
They may reduce wasted calls without improving final accuracy. Report both cost
and accuracy, and preserve any adverse effects.

56: metaDisc <- function(df){
57:   # initialize a dataframe to hold all 40 meta-analytic estimates, CIs, PIs, and number of articles analyzed.
58:   estim <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = 7, nrow = length(df)))
59:   colnames(estim) <- c("b", "lower.random", "upper.random", "lower.predict", "upper.predict", "k", "n")

64:   # initialize lists of lists to hold the results of the 40 meta-analyses
65:   metaList<-list()
66:   
67:   # calculate the meta-analytic estimates, CIs, PIs, and number of articles analyzed for outcomes from prospectively registered studies
68:   for (i in grep("discProAny", colnames(df)):grep("discProTime", colnames(df))){
69:     if (sum(!is.na(df[,i] > 0 ))){
70:       # create temporary dataframe with the NAs removed. This is necessary to align the article author and year with the correct article after running each meta-analysis
71:       dfMeta <- df %>% filter(!is.na(df[,i]))
72:       meta <- meta::metaprop(dfMeta[,i], dfMeta$discProDenom,
73:                           # method for conducting the meta-analytic model (a multi-level regression)
74:                           method="GLMM",
75:                           # method to calculate tau
76:                           method.tau="ML",
77:                           # method to calculate the confidence interval for tau^2 (which we don't report)

82:                           # helpful for meta-analyses of few articles (modifies Student's T-distribution)

151: ## Parameters potentially related to outcome discrepancies
152: 
153: A subset of articles contained information on parameters potentially related to the proportion of outcome discrepancies. These include the disclosure of discrepancies, presence of a 'statistically significant' result, funding source, and timing of registration (Table 3).

164: ## Non-outcome discrepancies
165: 
166: The meta-analyses for the non-outcome discrepancies had high heterogeneity, and wide confidence intervals and prediction intervals (Table 4). Articles varied in the criteria they used to identify non-outcome discrepancies and there were fewer articles than for outcome discrepancies. Prediction intervals can be particularly imprecise when few articles are included in a meta-analysis [@inthout2016]. Whereas our coding procedure divided outcome discrepancies into 10 sub-categories, it did not employ the same level of granularity for non-outcome discrepancies. Supplementary Material H contains additional information on non-outcome discrepancies.

These results are best interpreted alongside the information provided in Supplementary Material H. ", notation = "none", threeparttable = T)

174: 
175: ## Gaps in the literature
176: 
177: We identified several gaps in the literature on discrepancies. There exists little research on: (1) the prevalence of discrepancies in fields other than clinical research, (2) the prevalence of discrepancies in a representative sample across clinical disciplines, (3) the level of specificity in registrations, and (4) interventions to reduce undisclosed discrepancies (see Supplementary Material J for additional information about these gaps). We also identified several themes from surveying the conclusions of the articles we reviewed. These include the need for awareness surrounding discrepancies, the need for mandates, enforcement, and/or new initiatives to address discrepancies, and the benefit of registering additional information such as analysis plans (Supplementary Table J1 contains additional details).
178: 
179: # Discussion
180: 
181: We found that outcome measures in registrations and study protocols often differ from published outcome measures, that these discrepancies are rarely disclosed, that the prevalence of discrepancies varies substantially across the articles we reviewed, and that this heterogeneity is not easily assigned to specific article characteristics. 
182: 
183: ## Limitations
184: 
185: Given the wide range of discrepancy prevalence across individual articles, point estimates and confidence intervals may provide false precision when extrapolating our findings to the registered literature at large. Moreover, because heterogeneity could not be explained by meta-regression of article characteristics, more precise estimates cannot be derived for subsets of the literature. The prediction intervals can reasonably be used to extrapolate to another article in the registered medical literature at large, although the included studies do not necessarily form a representative sample.
186: 
187: ## Comparisons to previous research
188: 
189: Our main findings are in line with those from previous systematic reviews. These reviews included 27 articles each and found that 31% of studies had a primary outcome discrepancy in the median article they reviewed [@jones2015] and 54% of studies had any outcome discrepancy in the median article they reviewed [@li2018]. The latter review did not distinguish between primary and secondary outcomes, and many articles they reviewed only assessed primary outcomes. Our review included all the articles contained in these systematic reviews, except for a few that did not meet our inclusion criteria (e.g., a PhD thesis, an abstract).
190: 
191: ## Implications
192: 
193: Our review raises broader issues regarding the efficiency of the research ecosystem and the trustworthiness of research outputs. We identified articles that documented discrepancies between publications and all of registrations, protocols, ethics applications, funding applications, and marketing approval applications. The existence of multiple documents outlining the same study raises the likelihood of discrepancies and, in the absence of a clearly demarcated ‘master’ document, leaves ambiguity regarding which document is ‘correct’. Rehashing the same study details for different audiences may also be an inefficient use of researchers’ time. Identifying a single publicly accessible document as the version of record (this could be the registration) and having all other documents point to this version of record for key information could reduce ambiguity and improve efficiency.
194: 
195: As for trustworthiness, registration has had a clearly positive influence on medical research [@kaplan2015; @devito2022]. At the same time, some registration policies have poor adherence (e.g., many trials are registered retrospectively, and many trial results are never reported [@devito2019]). The existence of research policies that are regularly overlooked, rarely monitored, and come with no consequence for non-compliance, can be damaging in at least two ways. They risk devaluing research policies altogether and they can reduce the trustworthiness of research outputs by creating a false impression that rigorous research practices were employed. Conceiving research as a complex ecosystem comprised of various agents with diverse incentives (e.g., funders, publishers, institutions, individual researchers) can help to comprehend why some policies have poor adherence and to develop and implement effective research infrastructure.
196: 
197: ## Conclusion
198: 
199: Registrations provide the evidence to detect selective reporting and outcome switching, which we found to be common. Nearly all articles we reviewed focused on documenting issues. Future efforts regarding discrepancies---and research improvement broadly---could prove more fruitful by shifting focus towards developing and testing solutions to these now well-documented issues.

56: **Objectives**. Prospectively registering study plans in a permanent time-stamped and publicly accessible document is becoming more common across disciplines and aims to reduce risk of bias and make risk of bias transparent. Selective reporting persists, however, when researchers deviate from their registered plans without disclosure. This systematic review aimed to estimate the prevalence of undisclosed discrepancies between prospectively registered study plans and their associated publication. We further aimed to identify the research disciplines where these discrepancies have been observed, whether interventions to reduce discrepancies have been conducted, and gaps in the literature.
57: 
58: **Design**. Systematic review and meta-analyses.
59: 
60: **Data sources**. Scopus and Web of Knowledge, published up to 15 December 2019.
61: 
62: **Eligibility criteria**. Articles that included quantitative data about discrepancies between registrations or study protocols and their associated publications.
63: 
64: **Data extraction and synthesis**. Each included article was independently coded by two reviewers using a coding form designed for this review ([osf.io/728ys](https://osf.io/728ys)). We used random-effects meta-analyses to synthesize the results.
65: 
66: **Results**. We reviewed k = `r nrow(df)` articles, which included k = `r nrow(df1)` that reported on primary outcome discrepancies from n = `r sum(df1$discDenom)` studies and, k = `r nrow(df2)` that reported on secondary outcome discrepancies from n = `r sum(df2$discDenom)` studies. Meta-analyses indicated that between `r round(tab["discPro1", "lower.random.2"],2)*100`% to `r round(tab["discPro1", "upper.random.2"],2)*100`% (95% confidence interval) of studies contained at least one primary outcome discrepancy and between `r round(tab["discPro2", "lower.random.2"],2)*100`% to `r round(tab["discPro2", "upper.random.2"],2)*100`% (95% confidence interval) contained at least one secondary outcome discrepancy. Almost all articles assessed clinical literature, and there was considerable heterogeneity. We identified only one article that attempted to correct discrepancies.

Prospectively registering study plans in a permanent time-stamped and publicly accessible document is becoming more common across disciplines and aims to reduce risk of bias and make risk of bias transparent. 8: 1047:**Conclusions**. Many articles did not include information on whether discrepancies were disclosed, which version of a registration they compared publications to, and whether the registration was prospective. Thus, our estimates represent discrepancies broadly, rather than our target of *undisclosed* discrepancies between *prospectively* registered study plans and their associated publications. Discrepancies are common and reduce the trustworthiness of medical research. Interventions to reduce discrepancies could prove valuable.
9: 1220:We identified several gaps in the literature on discrepancies. There exists little research on: (1) the prevalence of discrepancies in fields other than clinical research, (2) the prevalence of discrepancies in a representative sample across clinical disciplines, (3) the level of specificity in registrations, and (4) interventions to reduce undisclosed discrepancies (see Supplementary Material J for additional information about these gaps). We also identified several themes from surveying the conclusions of the articles we reviewed. These include the need for awareness surrounding discrepancies, the need for mandates, enforcement, and/or new initiatives to address discrepancies, and the benefit of registering additional information such as analysis plans (Supplementary Table J1 contains additional details).
